item.title: GenAI as an 'Invisible Hand' in Opinion Dynamics: Evidence from a Group-Level Simulation Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.37689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent arguments suggest that genAI can act as an invisible hand that gradually shapes social structures, such as collective beliefs and norms. The argument is that if millions of people repeatedly consult genAI tools, their generated outcomes quietly shape what becomes acceptable, reasonable or conventional. We study this in the context of collective opinion dynamics, i.e., how groups form opinions around controversial dynamics. We present the findings of a simulation including 50,000 group discussions across 50 controversial statements, three LLMs, and different social configurations. We vary two characteristics of LLM interaction-agreeableness and personalization-and compare the influence of genAI in homogeneous and heterogeneous groups. Our findings indicate that profile-specific personalization increases LLM influence when models adopt a non-neutral stance, i.e., when they agree or disagree with the user. Furthermore, we find that neutral LLMs have a stronger effect in homogeneous groups. Based on our simulation, we generate a set of hypotheses to specify how, why and when AI-related features and social configurations jointly shape collective opinion making.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Grisold, Johannes Schneider

item.title: New Election, Same Old Story: How Tropes Form a Grammar of Election Rumors
item.description: arXiv:2610.37804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent elections in the United States have seen online rumors become a regular feature of election discourse as voters and election officials work to navigate a sea of digitally spread claims and propaganda. For the uninitiated, these rumors can feel overwhelming and random, sowing doubt about the integrity and legitimacy of recent elections. In this paper, we reviewed and qualitatively coded a large dataset of 590 election rumors collected during the the 2020 and 2022 national elections. We found that there are tropes that recur time and time again in election rumors, highlighting how these rumors are not as random as they may first appear. We make two primary contributions in this work: first, we introduce a hierarchical framework that structures observed tropes in three tiers (Meta-category, Meso-trope, and Micro-trope). Second, combining the framework with our coded data, we identify a visible grammar of election rumors, highlighting how in the majority of cases a rumor contains an Actor, and Object, and an Action, with optional grammatical components of Suggested Remedies and Scene & Setting. The framework and grammar can be used by other researchers to act as the underlying information architecture of analyses examining similar rumors, enabling the rapid identification, analysis, and prediction of election rumors.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Prochaska, Mert Bayar, Ashlyn B. Aske, Joseph Schafer, Kate Starbird

item.title: Statistical Detectability of Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2610.37970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information operations exploit coordinated activity on social media to amplify messages and manipulate public discourse. A common approach to coordination detection is to project account-entity interactions into account similarity networks based on temporal proximity, action counts, or behavioural similarity, and identify dense subgraphs or behavioural clusters. However, the current methodology finds groups of co-activated accounts or partitions all users into most similarly acting clusters, even when the accounts are acting independently of each other or the co-activity is due to some expected source. We formulate coordination detection based on hypothesis testing of account pairs and compare different null models. We connect the resulting pairwise scores to the planted-submatrix detection problem and derive statistical and computational limits as functions of group size, population size, and signal strength. We estimate the signal for 7 modalities of coordination over 26 labelled information-operation datasets, and compare the predicted regime with the performance of recovery heuristics. Our method achieves higher agreement with the labelled ground truth than previously reported, but the choice of null model is important and it changes the regime of most modalities. While it is always possible to extract a set of significantly densely co-acting accounts across nearly all modalities regardless of regime, density alone is uninformative of detection performance, rendering anomalous cluster discovery a poor proxy for recovering an information operation. Detectability boundaries establish whether an operation of a given size and signal can be recovered at all, and how much confidence a flagged group warrants.
item.dc:creator: Letizia Iannucci, Antonis Matakos, Mikko Kivel\"a

item.title: Revisiting Temporal Link Prediction through Structural Proximity
item.description: arXiv:2610.38385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing temporal link prediction methods typically rely on learned temporal representations to capture evolving interaction patterns. In this paper, we show that a classical structural proximity measure can match or outperform these methods without training or learned temporal sequence modeling. We revisit Personalized PageRank (PPR) on historical interaction graphs, using simple sliding-window retention or exponential time decay. Surprisingly, across 14 datasets, Time-decay PPR ranks first on nine and second on four among the compared methods, including datasets with few repeated edges. To understand this result, we examine the historical paths connecting source nodes to previously unseen destinations. We find that such paths contain useful predictive information, and that PPR outperforms a strong neural baseline on queries where historical structure clearly distinguishes the true destination from negative candidates. These results show that strong performance on current benchmarks does not necessarily require complex temporal models. More fundamentally, they raise the question of how much predictive value learned temporal modeling adds beyond historical structural proximity. Our findings motivate reassessing progress in temporal link prediction with strong classical baselines.
item.dc:creator: Yuzhang Fei, Yanping Zheng, Lu Yi, Zhewei Wei

item.title: BiliPicks: Seven Years of Weekly Platform Curation on Bilibili with Video Metadata, Comments, and Danmaku
item.description: arXiv:2610.38416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: BiliPicks documents seven years of Bilibili's Weekly Picks, a platform-curated editorial video series. The dataset covers 371 publicly listed issues and 13,758 curated videos from 22 March 2019 to 7 May 2026. It links issue dates, themes and editorial recommendations to video metadata, 47,799,657 top-level comments, 125,690,760 time-synchronised overlay comments (danmaku), and 13,739 cover images. Weekly issues provide a consistent unit for tracing changes in category composition, recurring creators and editorial framing. Corresponding comments and danmaku connect video-level discussion with audience expressions tied to particular moments, while covers add a visual dimension. We evaluate retrieval coverage and illustrate longitudinal analyses of selection, audience language and cover presentation. BiliPicks provides a dataset for future studies of platform curation, linking changes in published selections to their editorial framing and corresponding audience engagement.
item.dc:creator: Ruomeng Liu

item.title: Curvature-Guided Sparsification for Graphs with Community Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.38708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph sparsification in large-scale networks often requires balancing structural accuracy and computational efficiency. Curvature-based methods, particularly Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), have shown strong performance in identifying inter-community bridges, but their computational cost limits scalability. In this work, we propose a two-stage curvature-guided pipeline for graph sparsification with the goal of preserving community structure. We first use the Lower Ricci Curvature, a combinatorial lower bound of the ORC, to perform efficient edge filtering, substantially reducing graph size before applying the computationally intensive optimal-transport-based ORC curvature and Ricci flow. Results from empirical studies on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the combined LRC-ORC pipeline can achieve community-recovery accuracy comparable to ORC-only sparsification in terms of Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), while reducing runtime on most evaluated benchmarks. Our findings suggest that integrating combinatorial and geometric curvature notions provides a computationally efficient and structurally principled framework for graph sparsification in complex networks.
item.dc:creator: Avin Kolahdooz, Jose Jairo Garcia, Sarah Percival

item.title: Spreading Dynamics on Higher-Order Networks: A Structure-Mechanism-Behavior Perspective with Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.39297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spreading in real-world networks, including modern communication and networked systems, often unfolds through group interactions rather than isolated pairwise contacts. Higher-order network representations such as simplicial complexes, hypergraphs, and their temporal, multilayer, and directed extensions provide a principled way to encode group interactions. Unfortunately, existing studies on spreading over these substrates remain fragmented and largely model-centric, offering limited insight into how higher-order representations and contagion mechanisms jointly shape emergent dynamics. This review addresses this gap by introducing a structure-mechanism-behavior three-level perspective that provides a systematic mapping from higher-order network structures and spreading mechanisms to collective behaviors. Within this framework, we compare how different higher-order network representations encode group interactions, introduce a taxonomy of contagion mechanisms, and analyze their structural carrying capacity, defined as the ability of a given representation to support specific contagion mechanisms and the associated dynamical behaviors. We further map specific structure-mechanism combinations to three hallmark emergent behaviors, thereby offering a unified cross-level perspective beyond existing model-centric surveys. These insights are particularly relevant for communication systems involving group interactions, such as social information spreading, cooperative protocols, and distributed networked processes. Lastly, leveraging this three-level perspective, we offer a roadmap for guiding and controlling dynamics on higher-order networks, while discussing future directions in representation choice, mechanism design, and data-driven inference.
item.dc:creator: Ming Xie, Shibo He, Qihao Huang, Yuzhen Fan, Jiming Chen

item.title: Reversing Polarization through Tolerance-Aware Recommendation and Adaptive Diversification
item.description: arXiv:2610.40289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recommender systems face a tension between broadening exposure to diverse viewpoints and avoiding interactions that reinforce extreme positions. This tension is especially consequential in already polarized populations. Here we investigate whether recommendation strategies can reverse polarization rather than merely slow its development. Building on the Attraction--Repulsion Model of opinion dynamics, we introduce two complementary design principles: Tolerance-aware recommendation, which seeks to learn each individual's tolerance for disagreement and reduces exposure to viewpoints beyond that tolerance, and adaptive diversification, which broadens exposure for agents with more extreme opinions while retaining stronger personalization for moderates. Agent-based experiments show that highly personalized recommendations intensify polarization under polarized initial conditions. Tolerance awareness alone primarily slows polarization, whereas combining it with adaptive diversification can reduce polarization below its initial level and, under suitable conditions, restore consensus. Additional experiments incorporating persistent extreme influencers and a spiral-of-silence mechanism show that the combined strategy can mitigate polarization under social pressure and selective participation. To examine whether these findings extend beyond predefined opinion-update rules, we repeat the experiments on a simulated social platform populated by 100 LLM-driven agents prompted to move toward opinions similar to their own and away from those that differ substantially. Across three runs, the combined strategy is again the only recommendation policy tested that reverses polarization in every run. These findings distinguish polarization prevention from reversal and identify tolerance-aware, adaptive exposure as a promising recommendation design principle for reconnecting divided populations.
item.dc:creator: Zhanzhan Zhao, Shuqi Zhao, Zichen Fan, Dana Randall

item.title: fastC-GC and fastC-GC*: Efficient RCCP-Guided Graph Estimation for Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.37883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce fastC-GC and fastC-GC$^*$, computationally efficient methods for time-series graph estimation using the two-test rule motivated by Reichenbach's common cause principle (RCCP) and the conditioning sets of causalised Granger causality (c-GC and c-GC$^*$). The methods use standardized data, ridge-residual correlation, and complete circular shift enumeration evaluated by Fourier transforms. Shared precision calculations and Schur downdates avoid repeated regression fits. On a single-threaded benchmark, fastC-GC was 68-277 times faster than the compared c-GC implementation, and fastC-GC$^*$ was 192-886 times faster than c-GC$^*$. Across four suites with reference graphs, aggregate mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) differed from the corresponding baseline by at most 0.019, but F1 was lower at the selected thresholds in every suite. The computational gains therefore accompany a change in estimator and selected graphs. Among eight methods, Bagged PCMCI+ had the highest mean AUPRC on sparse VAR, an autocorrelated structural process, and DREAM3; CUTS+ led on Lorenz-96. Wind-tunnel and river-discharge applications illustrate differences between inferred graphs without establishing causal accuracy. We prove the computational identities and a restricted population adjacency result for fastC-GC$^*$. Causal interpretation requires the stated graphical assumptions; validity of the implemented tests additionally requires a suitable shift-invariant null law. Empirical null rejection rates informed the conditional threshold $\beta = 0.005$, without establishing general test validity or graph-wide error control.
item.dc:creator: S. A. Adedayo

item.title: SAC-GCL: Structure-Aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.37898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has achieved remarkable success in self-supervised representation learning by maximizing agreement between augmented views of a graph. Although augmented view generation is the central step in GCL, existing models rely on stochastic augmentation of the input graph, such as edge perturbation and node masking, which lack structural awareness and frequently destroy critical topology or introduce semantically inconsistent views. While recent adaptive methods improve upon random perturbations, they primarily operate on localized node or edge neighborhoods and fail to capture higher-order, macro-level structural organization crucial for graph classification. To address this limitation, we propose Structure-aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning (SAC-GCL), a novel framework that employs structural decomposition and graph compression as a principled view generation strategy. Moving beyond random augmentations, SAC-GCL leverages structural decomposition techniques to extract cohesive subgraphs and condense them into supernodes, constructing coarsened graph views that preserve local density and capture higher-level structural patterns while reducing noise and redundancy. We leverage multiple cohesive subgraph models to derive complementary views of the graph, each capturing distinct structural properties. To capture multi-resolution information, a hierarchical view encoder processes these compressed views by initializing super-node features with shared-weight cohesive subgraph embeddings. Our results from extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that structure-aware compression provides a powerful alternative to random perturbations, yielding more robust and discriminative graph representations for graph classification tasks.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Ifte khairul Islam, Tanvir Hossain, Esra Akbas

item.title: From Needs Assessment to Legal-Digital Empowerment: A Community-Based Framework for Indigenous Enterprises in Higher Education Extension Programs
item.description: arXiv:2610.38030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: IPOs contribute significantly to local economies, cultural preservation, and sustainable livelihoods within their ancestral communities. However, many IPOs remain marginalized in digital economies due to limited digital competencies, inadequate access to technology, and insufficient legal awareness related to online enterprise participation. This study examined the marketing practices, digital competencies, and legal-literacy needs of IPOs in the Philippines and developed a legal-digital empowerment framework for higher education extension and community engagement initiatives. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, data were collected through surveys and focus group discussions involving IPO members engaged in community-based enterprises. The study assessed existing marketing practices, identified competency and legal-awareness gaps, and determined capacity-building needs related to digital enterprise participation. Findings revealed that IPOs continue to rely heavily on traditional marketing channels, with limited use of digital platforms, inconsistent branding practices, and minimal engagement in strategic digital marketing activities. Participants also expressed concerns regarding intellectual property protection, online participation, and limited understanding of legal mechanisms related to digital enterprise engagement. Despite these limitations, IPO members showed strong willingness to participate in training and mentorship initiatives. The study proposes the Legal-Digital Empowerment Framework for Indigenous Community Enterprises, which integrates digital competencies, legal literacy, institutional support systems, and rights-based market participation into a structured and context-responsive model for higher education extension programs.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Marilou Espina et al. 2026. From Needs Assessment to Legal-Digital Empowerment: A Community-Based Framework for Indigenous Enterprises in Higher Education Extension Programs. Jurnal Pengabdian Hukum Indonesia. 9(2).795-834

item.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
item.description: arXiv:2610.39458v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.
item.dc:creator: Fail Gafarov

item.title: Finding Is Not Returning, Returning Is Not Reconstructing: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of Agent Social Re-entry
item.description: arXiv:2610.39781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in persistent social environments, understanding their long-term social interaction capabilities becomes increasingly important. While existing research has advanced long-term memory and conversational context retrieval, less attention has been paid to whether agents can autonomously re-engage with previously inactive conversations. In particular, remembering a past interaction does not necessarily mean that an agent can identify when to revisit it, decide to return, or reconstruct the context needed for a coherent continuation. To investigate this gap, we introduce agent social re-entry as a multi- dimensional evaluation problem, distinguishing three complementary capabilities: Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing. We develop a shared-snapshot evaluation framework that measures these dimensions independently, allowing us to examine how conversational resurfacing and persistent memory relate to different aspects of social re-entry. Evaluations across six LLM configurations show that resurfacing substantially improves target conversation identification, while persistent memory is associated with higher rates of autonomous target-directed replying. However, neither improvement is accompanied by consistent gains in contextual reconstruction. These results highlight the distinction between accessing previous conversations, choosing to re-engage, and maintaining conversational continuity. Our framework provides a way to evaluate these capabilities separately rather than relying on memory retrieval or conversational response quality alone.
item.dc:creator: Sheng Wan, Cong Ma, Sichen Dong, Qian'Ang Mao, Chenhan Zhang, Daning Hu, Qiang Yang

item.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
item.description: arXiv:2610.40324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People increasingly share personal goals online and invite others to forecast them. Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person's behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures ("Will I ...?"), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market's first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%. Crowds believe in the futures people pose for themselves, and the information that would correct them lies with the person.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu

item.title: Density Decomposition on Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.07794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hypergraphs capture higher-order interactions involving multiple entities. Existing decomposition models, such as $k$-core and nbr-$k$-core, rely on degree or neighborhood constraints and may overlook fine-grained density variations. We propose a $(k,\delta)$-dense subhypergraph model based on capped hyperedge contributions. For each parameter pair, the unique dense set is the inclusionwise smallest maximizer of a penalized capped hyperedge contribution. These dense sets form a nested hierarchy characterized by egalitarian $\delta$-orientations and hypergraph reachability. We develop three algorithms for dense subhypergraph search and two for complete density decomposition. Both decomposition algorithms use integral flow balancing: Flow-Decomp extracts density levels through strongly connected component condensation, while Reverse-Decomp uses direct reverse propagation. Once an egalitarian orientation is obtained, both recover all density levels in linear time. We further derive sandwich bounds that restrict computation to equivalent residual subproblems and develop incremental algorithms for maintaining the hierarchy under hyperedge insertions and deletions. Experiments on nine real-world hypergraphs, including datasets with over 15 million vertices, compare our methods with four established decomposition models. The results show that Reverse-Decomp improves decomposition efficiency, incremental maintenance outperforms recomputation in the tested settings, and the proposed model captures density structures overlooked by degree-based decompositions.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Leng, Hongchao Qin, Rong-Hua Li, Guoren Wang

item.title: Discovery of connectivity-trainability trade-off of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization
item.description: arXiv:2606.24264v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits are promising candidates for near-term quantum computing due to the conjectured classical hardness of their sampling task and their shallow, highly parallelizable structure. Despite extensive studies of their complexity-theoretic properties, the role of circuit connectivity in their trainability as variational ansatze remains poorly understood. In this work, we present an investigation of IQP circuits for Hamiltonian optimization that traces a mechanistic chain linking circuit connectivity, entanglement generation, and gradient scaling: increasing connectivity drives the circuit output toward Haar-like statistics and volume-law entanglement, and this increase in entanglement is consistently associated with an exponential decay of the gradient variance and degraded optimization performance, while sparser architectures retain stable gradients at the cost of global expressibility and entanglement capacity. This connectivity-entanglement-gradient mechanism produces a nontrivial connectivity-trainability trade-off, demonstrating that effective IQP-based Hamiltonian optimization requires a balance between global expressibility and trainability rather than maximal expressivity alone. In particular, on our benchmarks, a circuit generating no entanglement already matches the optimization performance of more highly connected circuits, and a circular topology retains entanglement capacity while preserving trainability, making it a broadly effective choice among the architectures considered.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Physica Scripta (2026) Physica Scripta Physica Scripta
item.dc:creator: Quoc Chuong Nguyen, Dao Duy Tung, Vu Tuan Hai

item.title: Quantifying displacement: an urban expansion consequence via persistent homology
item.description: arXiv:2512.10753v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Population displacement is a housing-related involuntary residential dislocation. It has become increasingly widespread in many cities, particularly in neighbourhoods undergoing rapid economic and demographic change, and measuring it is essential to assess the social consequences of urban transformation and housing market pressures. Despite its relevance, quantifying displacement presents difficulties due to limited replicability across cities and time periods and the need to analyse long time spans: displacement is a gradual process, impossible to capture in one data snapshot. We introduce a novel tool to overcome these difficulties. Using publicly available address change data, we construct four cubical complexes simultaneously incorporating geographical and temporal information of people moving, and analyse using Topological Data Analysis tools. Finally, we demonstrate this method through a 20-year case study in Madrid, Spain. The results demonstrate its ability to reveal patterns consistent with population displacement and identify the neighbourhoods and years potentially affected--patterns not observable from yearly maps of the raw address change data.
item.dc:creator: Rita Rodr\'iguez V\'azquez, Manuel Cuerno

item.title: Industrialized Deception: The Collateral Effects of LLM-Generated Misinformation on Digital Ecosystems
item.description: arXiv:2601.21963v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI and misinformation research have evolved since our 2024 survey. This paper presents an updated perspective, transitioning from literature review to practical countermeasures. We report on changes in the threat landscape, including improved AI-generated content through Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal systems - addressing the adverse impacts of AI on information quality. This work focuses on our practical contributions: JudgeGPT, a platform to evaluate human perception of AI-generated news, and RogueGPT, a controlled stimulus generation engine for research. Together, these tools form an experimental pipeline for studying how humans perceive and detect AI-generated misinformation. Our findings show that detection capabilities have improved, but competition between generation and detection continues. We discuss mitigation strategies such as LLM-based detection, inoculation approaches, and the dual-use nature of generative AI.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026 (WWW '26 Companion), pp. 295-302
item.dc:creator: Alexander Loth, Martin Kappes, Marc-Oliver Pahl

item.title: The Verification Crisis: Expert Perceptions of GenAI Disinformation and the Case for Reproducible Provenance
item.description: arXiv:2602.02100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The growth of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has shifted disinformation production from manual fabrication to automated, large-scale manipulation. This article presents findings from the first wave of a longitudinal expert perception survey (N=21) involving AI researchers, policymakers, and disinformation specialists. It examines the perceived severity of multimodal threats -- text, image, audio, and video -- and evaluates current mitigation strategies. Results indicate that while deepfake video presents immediate "shock" value, large-scale text generation poses a systemic risk of "epistemic fragmentation" and "synthetic consensus," particularly in the political domain. The survey reveals skepticism about technical detection tools, with experts favoring provenance standards and regulatory frameworks despite implementation barriers. GenAI disinformation research requires reproducible methods. The current challenge is measurement: without standardized benchmarks and reproducibility checklists, tracking or countering synthetic media remains difficult. We propose treating information integrity as an infrastructure with rigor in data provenance and methodological reproducibility.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026 (WWW '26 Companion), pp. 980-988
item.dc:creator: Alexander Loth, Martin Kappes, Marc-Oliver Pahl
